newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina recalls cold of still-distant Falklands.
newsitem.headline: Argentina recalls cold of still-distant Falklands.

text.p: Argentina recalled "the cold, permanent drizzle, the bombings" of the Falklands on Wednesday on the 15th anniversary of its war with Britain, its determination to win the South Atlantic islands still intact.

But Argentine hopes that a likely change in government in Britain would advance its 164-year-old sovereignty claim have faded since the opposition Labour Party clearly stated that if it wins May's vote, there will be "no discussion."

Sad ceremonies marked the day in 1982 when army dictator Gen. Leopoldo Galtieri sent commandos to the windswept Falklands to overpower a small British garrison and clear the way for a full-scale Argentine occupation.
Britain responded by sending a powerful naval task force. About 1,000 servicemen, mostly Argentines, died in a 10-week war that saw Britain restore its colonial rule dating from 1833.

Argentine army chief Gen. Martin Balza, then an artillery officer, wrote in Clarin newspaper of his memories of "the cold, permanent drizzle, the bombings and gray skies" and of surrender June 14 "feeling pain, anger, shame and sadness."
Using the islands' Spanish name, he wrote: "The Malvinas are pain, frustration, hope, the Malvinas are a feeling."

President Carlos Menem tries to keep that hope alive with an oft-repeated promise the Argentine flag will fly over the Falklands by 2000 -- not with more bloodshed but by diplomacy following the restoration of diplomatic links with Britain in 1989.
He has said Argentines should be encouraged by Hong Kong's return to China in June after 150 years of British colonial rule.
Defence Minister Jorge Dominguez said on Wednesday Menem wanted to attend the Hong Kong handover "because he hopes the same situation could happen with our country."
Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella in a letter to the 17,000 Argentine veterans of the Falklands war said Hong Kong showed "you need patience and tenacity to regain sovereignty."

But one British official pointed out on Wednesday there were "fundamental differences" between Hong Kong and the Falklands, not the least Britain's 99-year lease on China's New Territories which expires this year.
"Argentina is not China and the Malvinas are not Hong Kong," Argentine foreign relations expert Carlos Escude wrote in La Nacion newspaper.

While people like Escude who publicly state "the Malvinas will never be Argentine again" are a minority, diplomats say there is "more willingness to consider alternative ideas -- like Menem considering shared sovereignty."
Britain, which refuses any discussion of sovereignty at all, flatly rejected the Peronist president's suggestion early this year that both flags could one day fly over the islands.
But the two former foes are cooperating on oil exploration and trying to end a fishing quarrel. The 2,200 fiercely pro-British islands have even allowed more Argentines to visit war graves.
"The islanders still don't trust Argentina," said one foreign diplomat. "But it has done well showing it is no longer the Argentina of 1982, the Argentina of Galtieri."
